"Contemporary" means belonging to the same period of time. That period could be the present — right now, today — or it could be any other specific era in history. This one idea is the seed from which all meanings of the word grow.

"Contemporary" carries two closely related meanings, and understanding the difference between them is the key to mastering this word.

Meaning 1: Of the present time (modern, current)

This is the meaning most people encounter first. When you say something is "contemporary," you often simply mean it belongs to right now — to today's world.

  • Contemporary music = music being made in today's era
  • Contemporary fashion = the styles people wear now
  • Contemporary issues = problems and topics that are relevant today
  • A contemporary novel = a novel written in recent times

Think of it this way: if something feels fresh, current, and of this moment in history rather than belonging to a past era, it is contemporary.

Meaning 2: Existing or happening at the same time as something (or someone) else

This is the older and more precise meaning. Here, "contemporary" does not necessarily mean "modern." It just means two things existed or occurred during the same time period — whatever that period happens to be.

  • Shakespeare and Galileo were contemporary figures. (They lived at the same time, in the late 1500s/early 1600s.)
  • The two wars were contemporary events. (They happened at the same time.)
  • Dickens was contemporary with Tolstoy. (They were alive and writing during the same era.)

Notice that in this sense, both Shakespeare and Galileo are "contemporary" with each other even though they lived over 400 years ago. The word here is about simultaneity — the relationship between two things in time — not about being modern.
How to Tell Which Meaning Is Being Used

Context always makes this clear.

When "contemporary" is paired with "with" — as in "contemporary with" — it almost always signals Meaning 2. You are comparing two things and saying they coexisted in the same time period.

When "contemporary" stands alone before a noun — contemporary art, contemporary society, contemporary design — it almost always signals Meaning 1, meaning current or modern.
The Crucial Insight: Time Is Relative

Here is something that trips many learners up, but once you grasp it, the word clicks completely.

"Contemporary" is always relative to a reference point.

When a historian studies Ancient Rome and mentions "contemporary accounts," they do not mean accounts written today. They mean accounts written at the time of Ancient Rome — accounts that were contemporary with the events being studied.

So the word floats across all of history. It attaches itself to whatever time period is being discussed and means "of that same time."

  • If you are discussing the year 1800, "contemporary thinkers" means thinkers of 1800.
  • If you are discussing today, "contemporary thinkers" means thinkers of today.

The reference point shifts, and "contemporary" moves with it.

These two words are often used interchangeably in everyday speech, and that is perfectly fine. However, in certain fields — especially art, architecture, and design — they carry distinct technical meanings.

Modern (in art/architecture) refers to a specific movement and era, roughly from the late 1800s to the mid-1900s. Think of Picasso, Le Corbusier, minimalist architecture, abstract expressionism.

Contemporary (in art/architecture) refers to what is happening right now — art and design from roughly the 1970s/80s to the present. It is more experimental, diverse, and harder to pin to a single style.

Outside of these specialized fields, the distinction barely matters. In everyday conversation, saying "modern design" and "contemporary design" means essentially the same thing.

Beyond its dictionary definition, the word carries a certain feeling or tone. Calling something contemporary usually implies:

Relevance. A contemporary approach to a problem is one that fits today's world, today's tools, today's thinking. It is not stuck in the past.

Currency. Contemporary things are up-to-date. A contemporary artist is not painting in the style of the 1700s; they are working in a style that reflects the sensibility of the present moment.

Shared time. When applied to people, calling two individuals "contemporaries" carries a sense of shared experience — they inhabited the same world, breathed the same cultural air, faced the same events.

"Contemporary" pairs naturally with many nouns. Here are the most common, so you recognize them immediately when you encounter them:

Contemporary art / contemporary music / contemporary dance / contemporary literature / contemporary cinema — all referring to art forms being created in the present era.

Contemporary society / contemporary culture / contemporary life / contemporary world — the world as it exists right now.

Contemporary issues / contemporary problems / contemporary debates — matters that are relevant and live right now, not historical ones.

Contemporary with — used to say two things existed at the same time (e.g., "She was contemporary with the great Romantic poets").

Contemporary sources / contemporary records / contemporary accounts — in historical writing, these mean documents or records created at the time being studied, not modern ones.

"Contemporary" as an adjective means of the same time period — and that period is either (a) the present, or (b) whatever specific era is being discussed. When used alone, it usually means current and modern. When used with "with" or in a historical context, it means occurring or existing at the same time as something else. The word is always relative — it anchors itself to a reference point in time and means "belonging to that same moment."
